JobMediaInfo.description:
What the input actually was, as probed at submit.

This is the same probe the submit-time compatibility checks read, so it explains
rejections: an mp3 refused for an image output has no video stream here, and a still
refused for frames has no duration.

Every field is optional. The probe can be partial or absent — an unusual container, a
job submitted before this data was stored — and a missing field means "not reported",
never zero.

JobMediaVideoInfo.description:
The primary video stream.

width/height are DISPLAY dimensions — rotation already applied. A phone clip shot
portrait is commonly encoded 1920x1080 with rotation_deg=90, and every consumer that
reads the encoded dimensions instead gets the orientation wrong. encoded_* is kept
alongside for the cases that genuinely need the pre-rotation values.

get.description:
What each output type and preset requires of its input.

The same table the gateway enforces at submit, published so clients can validate
before sending rather than reimplementing the rules and drifting from them.

Unauthenticated: it is static product documentation, not account data.

Your account's jobs, newest first.

Scoped to the caller's account, same as GET /v1/jobs/{job_id}. Ordered by updatedAt
descending and paginated with an opaque cursor (the last job_id of the previous page)
rather than an offset, so rows are not skipped or repeated when jobs update mid-scan.

Rows omit the bundle download URL by design; fetch the single-job endpoint for that.

get.description:
Status, tier decision, usage and billing for a single job.

Scoped to the caller's account: the document is read from
db-accounts/{their account}/jobs/{job_id}, so a valid key for one account cannot
read another account's job — an unknown id and someone else's id both 404.

The response is built from an explicit allowlist. The stored document also holds
runner/lane internals, engine result URIs, the raw estimate and
deliveryAccess.bundleToken; none of those are returned. The bundle download URL IS
returned, because it is job-scoped, expiring, and the caller owns the job.

`media` is the exception that proves the rule: it is a curated view of
estimate.probe.input_media, built field by field in services/job_media.py rather than
passed through, so the rest of the estimate stays internal. It reports what the input
actually was, which is what makes a compatibility rejection self-explanatory.

get.description:
The forensic media report produced by the media_report_v1 preset.

The report also ships inside the outputs bundle; this serves it directly so a caller
does not have to download and unzip a bundle to read a few KB of JSON.

Account-scoped like the other job endpoints. 404 when the job exists but carries no
report, which means media_report_v1 was not among its outputs.

Returns the report inline when the worker stored it. Very large reports are kept out
of the job document, and the response then carries `download_url` instead — callers
should handle both.

get.description:
Moderation verdict for a job.

A separate endpoint rather than a field on GET /v1/jobs/{job_id} because the verdict
is the thing a moderation caller polls for, and it lets a client fetch it without
pulling billing and bundle detail on every poll.

Scoped to the caller's account exactly like the status endpoint: an unknown id and
another account's id both 404.

404 when the job exists but moderation was never requested. That is deliberate — a
200 with an empty body would be indistinguishable from "moderated and found nothing",
and for a moderation product those must never be confused.

The response is an allowlist AND the stored result is stripped on read. Job documents
written before the worker's sanitizer was fixed still contain the threshold table and
model names; see services/job_moderation.py.
